title: “BUT IT’S BIBLICAL!” — THE POLYGAMY ARGUMENT THAT COLLAPSES WHEN YOU READ THE WHOLE BIBLE
paragraphs:
“BUT IT’S BIBLICAL!” — THE POLYGAMY ARGUMENT THAT COLLAPSES WHEN YOU READ THE WHOLE BIBLE
Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had multiple wives. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So if the Bible records polygamy—and sometimes even regulates it—how can Christians say monogamy is God’s design? The answer is more uncomfortable, more beautiful, and far more Christ-centered than either side usually admits.
There is an argument spreading through conversations, comment sections, religious groups, and even Christian circles.
It sounds devastatingly simple.
“Polygamy is biblical.”
Then come the names.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
Then come the verses.
Exodus 21.
Deuteronomy 21.
2 Samuel 12.
And suddenly the Christian defending monogamy can feel trapped.
Because the verses are real.
The men are real.
The marriages are real.
And pretending those passages do not exist does nothing to defend the truth.
So we are not going to hide from them.
We are going straight into them.
Because Christians should never be afraid of a Bible verse.
But there is one question we must ask before allowing anyone to build a theology from a biblical story:
Does the Bible recording something mean the Bible is recommending it?
That question changes everything.
Scripture records murder.
Scripture records incest.
Scripture records deception.
Scripture records adultery.
Scripture records drunkenness.
Scripture records slavery.
Scripture records kings who rebel against God and disciples who abandon Jesus.
Nobody reasonably concludes that because an event occurs inside the Bible, the event therefore represents God’s ideal.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity.
That is part of its power.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It shows Abraham afraid.
Jacob deceptive.
David adulterous.
Solomon compromised.
Peter denying Christ.
The Bible is not a collection of flawless people demonstrating flawless behavior.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing deeply flawed people.
And that distinction matters enormously when discussing polygamy.
To be precise, the Old Testament contains polygyny—the marriage of one man to multiple women. Mosaic legislation also addresses circumstances in which a man has more than one wife.

That means Christians should not make a careless claim such as, “Polygamy never existed among God’s people,” or, “The Old Testament contains an explicit universal law saying every Israelite man may have only one wife.”
Those claims would go beyond the text.
The stronger biblical argument is different.
Scripture can regulate a fallen human practice without presenting that practice as the creational ideal.
Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive key.
When religious leaders questioned Him about marriage and divorce, Jesus did something remarkable.
He did not begin with Abraham.
He did not begin with Jacob.
He did not begin with David.
He did not begin with Solomon.
He went behind all of them.
Back before Israel.
Back before Moses.
Back before kings.
Back before human culture had accumulated centuries of brokenness.
Jesus went to Eden.
He said:
“Have you not read that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female?”
Then Jesus cited Genesis:
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh.”
And then Christ declared:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
Do not rush past what Jesus just did.
When asked about the boundaries of marriage, Christ appealed to the beginning.
The Greek text of Matthew 19:5 contains a small phrase with enormous significance:
οἱ δύο — hoi dýo
“The two.”
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Jesus points His hearers toward God’s creation pattern: male and female, husband and wife, the two becoming one flesh.
And the Hebrew beneath the Genesis passage is equally beautiful:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-hayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24.
One flesh.
Not because marriage is merely a contract for sexual access.
Not because a woman is an addition to a man’s collection.
Not because marriage exists to maximize one person’s desires.
Biblical marriage is covenantal union.
And when Jesus wanted His audience to understand marriage, He deliberately took them back to the architecture of creation.
This becomes crucial because someone may immediately object:
“But Abraham had Hagar.”
Yes.
And what happened?
God had promised Abraham descendants through whom blessing would come. But Abraham and Sarah became impatient with the timing of that promise.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis 16 does not read like an advertisement for expanding the household.
It reads like a warning about what happens when frightened human beings attempt to manufacture with their own hands what God has promised by His power.
Abraham went in to Hagar.
She conceived.
And almost immediately the house fractured.

Genesis says that when Hagar realized she had conceived, her mistress became contemptible in her eyes. Sarah became furious. Abraham withdrew responsibility into Sarah’s hands. Hagar was treated harshly and fled.
A child would eventually stand in the middle of an agonizing household division.
Yes, God cared for Hagar.
Yes, God heard Ishmael.
That matters tremendously.
God's compassion toward Hagar and Ishmael should never be twisted into contempt for either of them.
But God showing mercy inside human brokenness is not the same thing as God declaring the brokenness His original design.
That distinction appears repeatedly throughout Scripture.
Then there is Jacob.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban’s deception, he first received Leah.
Then Rachel.
Then Bilhah.
Then Zilpah.
And what follows?
Read Genesis 29 and 30 slowly.
Do not merely count the wives.
Count the tears.
Count the jealousy.
Count the competition.
Count the desperation.
Leah longs to be loved.
Rachel envies her sister.
Children become entangled in a painful struggle for affection and status.
Even mandrakes become bargaining currency in the competition for Jacob’s attention.
This is one of the great mistakes people make when reading Scripture.
They see multiple wives and stop reading.
Keep reading.
The consequences are part of the story.
The Bible does not need to place a warning label after every dysfunctional relationship when the narrative itself is showing you the devastation.
Then there is Elkanah.
First Samuel 1 introduces Hannah and Peninnah.
Again, two women attached to one man.
Again, rivalry.
Again, anguish.
Peninnah provokes Hannah because Hannah has no children.
Hannah weeps.
She cannot eat.
Her soul is bitter with grief.
Elkanah loves her, but his affection cannot erase the structure of rivalry surrounding the household.
Once again:
Do not just count wives.
Count tears.
Then comes David.
This is where defenders of biblical polygamy sometimes point to 2 Samuel 12:8, where God, speaking through Nathan, describes what had been given into David’s hands, including Saul’s house and wives.
That passage deserves serious treatment rather than evasion.

The language occurs in Nathan’s indictment after David has taken Bathsheba and arranged Uriah’s death. The point is that David had already received abundance and nevertheless coveted and seized what was not his.
But the existence of royal wives in David’s household does not erase another command already written into Israel’s Torah.
Long before David sat on a throne, God warned Israel concerning its future king:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim
“He shall not multiply wives for himself.”
Deuteronomy 17:17.
And why?
“that his heart turn not away.”
Then Solomon arrives.
And suddenly the warning becomes almost terrifying.
First Kings 11 says Solomon loved many foreign women and eventually possessed seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.
If quantity were proof of divine approval, Solomon would become the champion of the argument.
Instead, Scripture makes him the warning.
His wives turned his heart after other gods.
The king famous for wisdom became living evidence that knowing truth does not make a person immune to disobedience.
That should frighten every one of us.
Because this article is no longer merely about polygamists.
It is about us.
It is about the frightening human ability to find religious language for something our hearts already want.
We can search Scripture not because we want Scripture to correct us, but because we desperately want a verse that will protect us from correction.
And if we search long enough without respecting context, covenant, genre, redemptive history, and the whole counsel of God, almost anything can begin to sound “biblical.”
That is why the statement “The Bible regulates polygamy” requires careful thinking.
Yes, Mosaic law contains regulations involving plural marriages.
Exodus 21:10, for example, protects a woman’s rights if another wife is taken.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance where a man has two wives.
Those texts are there.
We should not erase them.
But regulation does not automatically equal idealization.
The Torah governed real Israelites living in a fallen social world. Some laws restrained injustice and protected vulnerable people within circumstances that were already less than Eden.
And Jesus gives us a powerful example of this distinction with divorce.
In Matthew 19, His opponents appeal to Moses.
Jesus answers:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read those final words again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
That sentence teaches us something profound about biblical interpretation.
Something may be tolerated or regulated within fallen human conditions without representing the pattern established at creation.
So when we ask what marriage is supposed to be, Jesus does not tell us merely to catalogue every marriage practiced by every Old Testament figure.
He points backward:
Beginning.
Male and female.
Man and wife.
Two.
One flesh.
And then the New Testament continues speaking of marriage in strikingly singular terms.
Paul writes:
1 Corinthians 7:2.
He tells husbands:
“love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Ephesians 5:25.
Then Paul reaches back to Genesis 2:24:
“For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.”
Ephesians 5:31.
And suddenly marriage becomes even bigger than marriage.
Paul says:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Ephesians 5:32.
There it is.
The center is Jesus.
Christian marriage is not ultimately about maximizing romantic possession.
It is meant to testify to covenant faithfulness.
Christ and His Church.
Sacrificial love.
Faithfulness.
Union.
A husband is not called to imitate Solomon collecting women.
He is called to imitate Jesus giving Himself.
That changes the question from:
“How many women can I biblically justify having?”
to:
“How can my marriage tell the truth about Christ?”
Those are radically different questions.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because polygamy is not the only subject on which people ask, “How far can I go and still call myself biblical?”
We do it with lust.
We do it with money.
We do it with unforgiveness.
We do it with pride.
We do it with sexual sin.
We do it with bitterness.
We do it with relationships.
We do it with ambition.
Sometimes we are not asking God, “What is Your heart?”
We are asking, “Where is the technical boundary beyond which You can finally tell me no?”
There is a dangerous way to hold a Bible.
You can hold it open while keeping your heart closed.
You can know verses while resisting their Author.
You can win an argument and lose the very thing Scripture was trying to expose inside you.
So to the polygamist who says, “But Abraham did it,” the Christian response should never be mockery.
It should be:
Abraham needed grace too.
To the person who says, “Jacob did it”:
Jacob needed grace too.
“David did it.”
David desperately needed grace too.
“Solomon did it.”
And Solomon discovered that extraordinary wisdom does not make rebellion safe.
That is the scandal running through Scripture.
God works through broken people without calling their brokenness good.
And that is incredibly good news.
Because if God only worked through people whose histories were spotless, none of us would have hope.
The Bible's heroes are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Abraham cannot save you.
Jacob cannot save you.
David cannot save you.
Solomon cannot save you.
And your ability to defend your lifestyle with carefully selected verses cannot save you either.
Only Christ can.
Maybe you have used Scripture to defend something God has been trying to confront.
Maybe your issue has nothing to do with polygamy.
Maybe nobody knows what your issue is.
Maybe you have become extraordinarily skilled at giving spiritual names to things that are slowly destroying you.
God is not asking you to become better at hiding.
He is calling you into the light.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you away from the cliff.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
Grace says sin mattered so much that Christ carried it to a cross.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die merely to make our chosen lifestyles more comfortable.
He died to forgive sinners, reconcile us to God, and transform people who could never rescue themselves.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the same Jesus who forgives also says:
“Follow me.”
That means sometimes following Him requires surrendering an argument we desperately wanted to win.
It may require saying:
“Lord, I used Your Word to defend myself instead of allowing Your Word to search me.”
That confession is not the end of your story.
It might be where your real story finally begins.
This is why our theme remains:
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin should be romanticized.
Not because every choice is equally biblical.
But because Jesus Christ specializes in meeting sinners inside stories that look irredeemable and writing something grace alone could write.
If this exposed something you have been defending, do not turn the comment section into a battlefield.
Turn it into an altar.

If you are wrestling with this teaching, say so honestly. Ask your question. Bring the verse you believe challenges this conclusion. We should be willing to examine Scripture together rather than fear difficult passages.
Somebody may need to discover that surrender did not destroy you.
Jesus met you there.
It does not.
Context matters.
Creation matters.
The whole counsel of Scripture matters.
And above everything else, Jesus matters.
Let them see that serious Christianity does not require pretending difficult passages do not exist.
But hear this carefully:
You do not earn salvation by supporting a Christian ministry.
You do not glorify God merely by clicking a button.
Jesus Christ purchased redemption—not us.

But if this ministry genuinely helps you glorify God, supporting it is one practical way you can help put more Christ-centered teaching, Scripture, discipleship resources, and Gospel truth in front of people who desperately need it.
Sharing costs nothing.
Following helps you stay connected.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to prove that you are righteous.
Not because Gospel Warrior is the Gospel.
But because if truth has helped you, passing truth forward can become an act of love toward someone who has not encountered it yet.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite Christians who have become spiritually tired.
Invite even the person who does not believe any of this yet.
Let them investigate Jesus for themselves.
Because at the end of this argument, the greatest danger is not simply misunderstanding polygamy.
It is learning how to quote the Bible without ever surrendering to the Christ the Bible reveals.
And perhaps that is the sentence that should follow you after you close this article:
The most dangerous Bible verse may be the one you use as a shield when Jesus intended it to become a mirror.
